name: Michael Dell
title: The Boy Who Out-Earned His Teacher
subtitle: How a Houston teenager who mined marriage records started a computer company in his dorm room with $1,000, stepped away, came back, and rebuilt it for the age of AI.
hook: At ==16==, Michael Dell took a job selling newspaper subscriptions by phone, and he noticed that the people who said yes were usually moving house or getting married. Marriage-licence applications were public in Texas. So he hired his friends, collected the addresses from the ==16 counties== around Houston, and mailed each couple a free trial offer. He made about **$18,000** in one year. When a school assignment asked for a tax return, he handed in his real one, and his teacher told him it had to be wrong: "You made more money than I did!" In November 2026, Forbes put his fortune at ==$228.5 billion==.

glance.label: Grew up
glance.value: Houston, the middle of three brothers. His father was an orthodontist, his mother a stockbroker and financial consultant.

glance.label: Education
glance.value: Biology, pre-med, at the University of Texas at Austin. He agreed with his parents to take one semester off in fall 1984, and left college for good.

glance.label: First job
glance.value: Age 12: dishwasher in a Chinese restaurant, then water boy, then assistant maître d'.

glance.label: First company
glance.value: PC's Limited, started with $1,000. Registered in January 1984 when he was 18, incorporated that May when he was 19.

glance.label: Main company today
glance.value: Dell Technologies, Round Rock, Texas. He is chairman and CEO, and the company had about 97,000 employees in January 2026.

glance.label: Source of wealth
glance.value: Dell Technologies, where he holds more than 50% of the votes for directors, plus DFO Management, his family's investment firm. Forbes estimate: $228.5 billion, world no. 4, on 1 November 2026.

glance.label: Family
glance.value: Married Susan Lieberman in 1989. They have four children and started the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation together in 1999.

glance.label: Known for
glance.value: Selling PCs direct to customers. In 1992, at 27, the youngest CEO ever to earn a Fortune 500 ranking. National Medal of Technology and Innovation, October 2026.

contact.howToReach: The only door with their names on it is the foundation's "Message to Michael and Susan Dell" form, so use that for a personal note, and write in public on his X or LinkedIn posts if you have something specific to add; neither route promises a reply. Do not pitch the family office, because DFO says it generally does not accept unsolicited proposals, business plans or ideas, and anything you send is not treated as confidential. The foundation does not fund individuals, never charges fees and never approaches individuals with awards, so treat any such message as a scam; organisations can share a project through its partnerships form, which lists India. Its scholarships are narrow: Dell Aspire Scholars is by college invitation at three Delhi colleges, Dell Scholars is for Texas high school seniors, and Dell Young Leaders supports students earning degrees across Africa. Keep your message under five lines: who you are, the one thing you built or measured, and the one clear thing you are asking for.

factCheck.method: Front matter and contact card built from primary records first: Dell Technologies' FY2026 10-K and 2026 proxy statement on SEC EDGAR, Dell's leadership, contact, investor and India pages, and the foundation's, DFO's and BDT & MSD's own sites. Childhood facts come from Michael Dell's own recorded 2008 interview with the Academy of Achievement, checked against a 1988 Christian Science Monitor profile, Encyclopedia.com's business-leader entry and the Franklin Institute. Every photo's author, licence and description came from the Wikimedia Commons API; photos were not opened and viewed, so captions rest on Commons metadata. Directory and data-broker listings were used as leads only, and nothing from them was kept.

disputed.claim: He earned $18,000 selling newspaper subscriptions in one year.
disputed.note: Dell said "about $18,000 in one year" in his 2008 interview, and Encyclopedia.com agrees. The Christian Science Monitor (1988) says $18,000 over two years. We use his own account.

disputed.claim: He sold $80,000 a month by the end of his freshman year.
disputed.note: The Christian Science Monitor and the Academy of Achievement both say $80,000 a month. Forbes's profile says he grossed $80,000 by the end of freshman year, and another Academy passage says $50,000 to $80,000 in upgrades and components without a time period. Not used on this card; chapter writers should choose the monthly figure and say so.

disputed.claim: Age when he started the company.
disputed.note: The foundation's bio says he founded it at 19 in 1984. The Academy dates the registration to January 1984, when he was 18, and the incorporation to May 1984, when he was 19. The glance entry gives both dates.

The Academy says the business was registered as PC's Limited, but also says it was incorporated in May 1984 as Dell Computer Corporation and renamed in 1988. The Franklin Institute also gives 1988. The Goodwill Computer Museum label on Commons says PC's Limited became Dell Computer Corp. in 1987. We do not state a renaming date on this card.

disputed.claim: Age when he bought and took apart his first Apple computer.
disputed.note: The Academy of Achievement says 15, while the Christian Science Monitor says 16 and some secondary sources say 14. Not used on this card.
Dell's US contact page lists 1 Dell Way, Round Rock, TX 78664. The 10-K and investor relations page list One Dell Way, Round Rock, Texas 78682. We use the SEC filing.

disputed.claim: Where he first ran the business.
disputed.note: The Daily Texan (2016) names Dobie 2713, while a book-summary site names a different dormitory. We use the Daily Texan. The Academy adds that he registered the company while operating from a condominium, so the dorm was only the first stage.
